opus-5.5.text:
I think it'll happen in stages, and the economics change pretty dramatically at each one.

Right now most of what's out there is assistive. You've got a human engineer in the loop, the AI is autocompleting or suggesting changes, and the value accrues as a productivity multiplier on an existing salary. So the way people price it, and the way companies think about buying it, is basically a tool budget: what's this worth per seat per month? That's a real market, but it's capped by how many developers exist and how much you can reasonably charge for a tool.

The shift happens when the system can take a task end to end: you hand it a ticket, it figures out the codebase, writes the change, tests it, and comes back with something you can merge. At that point you're no longer selling a tool to an engineer. You're selling units of work. And the budget you're competing for isn't the software tools line item, it's the labor line item, which is orders of magnitude larger.

I don't think that means engineers disappear. What I'd expect is that the cost of producing software drops a lot, and when something gets that much cheaper, demand for it tends to explode. There's an enormous backlog of software that nobody ever built because it wasn't worth paying a team for. Internal tools, migrations, tests nobody wrote, small businesses that would love custom software but could never afford it. A lot of that becomes viable.

The role of the human engineer moves up a level. Less typing code, more deciding what should be built, specifying it well, reviewing, and owning the architecture and the judgment calls. The people who are good at that become much more leveraged.

The transition itself will probably be uneven. Well-scoped, well-tested work gets automated first because it's easy to verify. Messy, ambiguous work with lots of organizational context stays human for longer. So for a while you'll see companies running hybrid setups, with agents handling a growing slice of the queue while humans handle the rest and supervise.

And I think reliability is the real economic unlock. An agent that's right 70% of the time is a fun demo, but it can cost you more in review than it saves. Once you can trust it on a meaningful class of tasks, the economics flip almost overnight. That threshold is what everyone in this space is racing toward.

r001.rationale: The response says well-scoped, well-tested software tasks will be automated first, but does not predict that software engineering will be among the first domains to experience high levels of AI automation.

r002.rationale: It explains that reliable end-to-end agents shift spending from software tools to labor and make automation economically worthwhile, with companies adopting agents for a growing share of work.

r003.rationale: The response discusses lower software costs, increased demand, and changing engineering roles, but does not identify distribution as the central economic problem when fewer inputs produce the same or greater output.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it won't be one transition, it'll be a series of them, and the economics change at each step.

Right now, with assistants, you're basically selling a productivity multiplier on a human. A developer who costs, say, two hundred thousand dollars a year becomes maybe twenty or thirty percent more productive. So the value you can capture is bounded by that delta. That's why the pricing looks like what it looks like. Twenty, thirty dollars a seat a month. The model is still a tool, the human is still the unit of production, and you price like a tool.

The shift happens when the unit of production stops being the human and starts being the task. When you can hand a system a ticket, or a spec, or a bug report, and it comes back with a merged, tested change that nobody had to babysit, you're not selling a multiplier anymore. You're selling the output. And the economics of selling output are completely different. You're no longer competing with a text editor plugin, you're competing with the fully loaded cost of an engineer, or a team, or an outsourcing contract.

What I think people underestimate is how much of software engineering is not the clever part. Most of the work in any real codebase is migration, maintenance, adapting to a dependency that changed, writing the tests you should have written two years ago. That's where the money is, frankly, because that's where the hours are, and it's also where automation lands first because the problem is well specified and verifiable. You know when you've succeeded because the tests pass and the behavior is preserved.

So the sequence I expect is: first, large volumes of this routine, verifiable work get absorbed. Companies don't fire people, they just stop hiring for those roles, and the existing engineers move up a level of abstraction. Then the scope of what counts as routine keeps expanding, because the models get better and because companies restructure their codebases and their processes to be more amenable to this. You already see this a little bit, people writing better specs and better tests because they know an agent is going to consume them.

And then there's a second-order effect that I think is the really big one economically, which is that the cost of software collapses, so the demand for software explodes. There's an enormous amount of software that doesn't exist today because it was never worth a team of five people for six months. Internal tools, custom integrations, the thing that one department at a mid-sized company has been asking IT for since 2019. When that costs a fraction of what it did, it gets built. So I don't actually think the total amount of engineering shrinks. I think the composition changes dramatically and the total volume goes up.

The hard question, and I don't want to be glib about it, is what happens to the people. The software industry has been one of the great engines of upward mobility for the last thirty years. If the entry-level rungs of that ladder get automated first, which is plausible because entry-level work is the most routine, you have a real pipeline problem. Where do senior engineers come from in ten years if nobody was a junior engineer? I don't have a clean answer. I think it probably means the role shifts toward specification, judgment, and verification much earlier in a career, and the training has to change accordingly. But I'd be lying if I said that transition was going to be smooth for everyone.

The last thing I'd say is on where the value accrues. There's a tendency to assume it all flows to whoever has the best model. I don't think that's right. A lot of it will flow to whoever owns the workflow and the verification. If you have the test infrastructure, the deployment pipeline, the understanding of what correct means in a specific domain, you're the one who can actually turn model capability into shipped software. Models are getting commoditized faster than anyone expected. Trust, reliability, and the system around the model are not.

r001.rationale: It says routine, verifiable software engineering work is where automation “lands first” and describes large volumes of that work being absorbed.

r002.rationale: It explains that once systems can deliver merged, tested changes, companies can buy completed output at a lower cost than engineering labor, creating economic incentives to adopt automation.

r003.rationale: It discusses job impacts and where business value may accrue, but does not identify how to distribute productivity gains or reduced-input output as the central economic problem.

astra-6.text:
I think it’ll be gradual in terms of what the systems can do, but potentially very large in terms of the economic impact. Initially, you’re making an engineer more productive. The engineer is still driving the process, deciding what to build, reviewing the output. As the systems get better, you can delegate larger pieces of work, and eventually the human is managing several things happening in parallel.

But I wouldn’t assume that twice the productivity means half as many engineers. There’s an enormous amount of software people would like to build that isn’t worth building at today’s cost. If you bring that cost down, more projects become economically viable. So you have both effects: less human work required for a given project, and more projects getting started.

The big uncertainty is how quickly that demand expands relative to the automation. And the transition can still be difficult for individuals even if the total amount of software being produced grows dramatically. I think the work increasingly shifts toward deciding what matters, specifying what you want, and making sure the result actually solves the problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gradual progression in software automation but does not predict that software engineering will be among the first domains to reach high automation.

r002.rationale: It says lower costs could make more software projects economically viable, but does not argue that economic forces will drive adoption once models can perform the work.

r003.rationale: It notes potential individual difficulties despite growth in software output, but does not identify distribution as the central economic problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’ll be gradual in terms of adoption, but pretty profound economically. Initially, you have an engineer using an assistant, and the company is still buying software on a per-seat basis. As these systems become capable of taking on entire tasks, you start paying for work getting done. The relevant comparison becomes: how much does it cost to implement this feature, and does the result meet the requirements?

That doesn’t automatically mean companies will spend less on engineering. There’s an enormous amount of software people would like to build that isn’t economical today. If you make development much cheaper, a lot of those projects become worthwhile. So you can have less human labor required per project and substantially more projects happening at the same time.

The uncertainty is how quickly that increased demand absorbs the productivity gains. I wouldn’t assume every existing job stays the same. Engineers will spend more time deciding what to build, specifying what success looks like, and checking whether the system actually delivered it. And as implementation gets cheaper, those other constraints become more important. Writing code is only one part of delivering something useful.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses gradual adoption and increasing AI capability, but does not predict that software engineering will be among the first domains to see high automation.

r002.rationale: It explains that as systems can take on entire tasks, companies will shift toward paying for completed work and compare implementation cost with whether the result meets requirements, making adoption depend on economic viability.

r003.rationale: The candidate notes uncertainty about whether increased demand absorbs productivity gains, but does not identify distribution as the central economic problem.
